Once you uploaded the graph - you get the difference with previously uploaded graphs, specifically, you will receive:

p_api_multi_1: Topology is built based on LSA1, LSA2, which are area only based. If a network has multiple areas, it is needed to save LSDB output from multiple devices and save it into separate files using the following format `Vendor name_protocol name.txt`
p_api_multi_2: For instance: there are two LSDBs `Cisco_ospf.txt`, `Juniper_ospf.txt`
p_api_multi_3: LSDBs are saved in `lsdb_samples` folder, then wrapped into LSDB attribute dictionary
p_api_upload_intro: Save the output from commands describing OSPF LSA1, LSA2, LSA5 and save it in the single file - cisco_lsdb_output.txt
p_api_upload_python: Using python we read the content of the file and push it (it's better to say - POST it) to the topolograph.
p_asym_1: Print out any asymmetric paths from different points of views.
p_asym_2: We get a list of nodes which have asymmetric paths. Just checking them - we can see difference in incoming and outgoing paths.
p_backup: In order to find out the backup path - just press on colored edge. You will simulate a link outage and the shortest path will be rebuilt passing by a 'failed' edge.
p_compare: When you perform some configuration changes (add new network, redistribute another protocol to OSPF or change filters in existed route-maps) it is highly desired to make sure that results of your action give you expected changes in OSPF network. In order to do this - upload your network before your changes and right after it and compare them. What will be shown:
p_cost_1: It's possible to change OSPF cost of any link. Right click on edge, new form pops up. Write new ospf cost in input field. Imagine if we need to redirect a traffic flow from 123.10.10.10 - 123.30.30.30 link to another link.
p_cost_2: Right click on colored edge and set 12. We get new traffic flow with new OSPF cost.
p_cost_change: Under `NetworkReactionOnFailure` tab it is possible to see a network reaction on a OSPF cost change on the fly. Set new OSPF cost in right-clicked edge menu.
p_dr_disabled: If neighbors do not have DR or they have, but they are only two neighbors on the link, and when we emulate edge failure - we remove the only a single link between two particular neighbors.
p_dr_disabled_mark: **Mark all shared media links (which have common DR) as disabled**
p_dr_enabled: Topolograph builds a topology based on OSPF adjacency and physical connectivity is hidden. But in some cases, we can assume that neighbors share the same media, in some cases - not. For example, if neighbors have a common DR - we assume that they are connected via shared physical media and then we emulate one of the edge failures between such neighbors - we emulate all edges down.
p_dr_enabled_mark: **Mark all shared media links (which have common DR) as enabled**
p_duplicated_example: 10.0.0.0/24 network is terminated on four nodes: 172.16.1.2, 172.26.1.2 and 172.30.2.1, 178.20.3.1 are directly connected, but not between each other.
p_duplicated_quote: "Analytics/Duplicated terminated networks. The issue with MPLS being affected by IP duplications in the network stems from the fact that labels are generated based on IP blocks, which can be duplicated. As a result, the same IP block may be associated with different labels. This leads to a situation where the same block, with different labels, is propagated to other routers, including the one with the duplicated IP. This becomes problematic when implementing MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) or Resource Reservation Protocol Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE), as it can degrade performance and lead to routing bugs in relation to MPLS-TE, among other issues. Therefore, the issue of block duplication across links is critical in MPLS environments, primarily due to the generation of duplicate labels for the same block. In routers, this causes confusion when recalculating the path for TE or RSVP-TE."
p_ecmp_1: We suggest that if we have multiple links bounded to ECMP and if the main link in ECMP goes down, the backup path should go via the second link in ECMP.
p_ecmp_2: If backup path goes not via ECMP and chooses completely different path - the report will be treated as failed.
p_gv_demo: Demo network has already uploaded for everyone. Press `Load dynamic graph` in order to upload it. Once you did it - you can see the topology, bold lines show ECMP links.

p_heatmap_1: Under `Analytics` tab it is possible to see how many terminated subnets are backuped via terminating the same subnet on different devices.
p_heatmap_2: Click on a node in order to find out which networks are backuped which not.
p_heatmap_3: As we can see only own device's loopback is not backuped - it is normal.
p_interarea: This report checks that if two locations are directly connected, backup paths should be only between two locations and do not go via third location as transit. Before running this report - it's needed to create groups (~site names/locations) and assign devices to groups. For example, there are two locations in France: the main site (EU_FRA) and the remote site (EU_FRA1). The same schema with offices in Italy. The main offices in France and Italy are connected to each other and have main (OSPF cost 10) and backup (OSPF cost 20) link.
p_interarea_failure: If the main link between main offices goes down - the backup path goes via remote offices!
p_interarea_remote: Remote offices have the main link (OSPF cost 1) to their main offices and backup link (OSPF cost 10) to the foreign office.

p_te_intro: What each vendor's parser turns into link attributes. A blank cell means the attribute is not read from that output, even when the router advertises it. A Watcher or BGP-LS session carries every attribute the router advertises.
p_term_1: How is it possible to know what networks are terminated on some particular node. There are two ways how to know about it. The first one - start typing Node ID in "Find node by RID/IP. Find network" field and you will see all terminated networks on the node.
p_term_2: The second method is just to press on a node. New form pops up with a list of all backuped and non-backuped networks. The network is treated as backuped if such network is terminated on min two nodes.

p_vrf_1: Multiple OSPF routing instances can exist on a single device in several VRFs. It causes nodes duplication on a visualisation graph. VRF tab allows to point multiple OSPF instances to a single one and avoid node duplication on a graph.
p_vrf_2: There are three VRFs and three OSPF instances on a router. In order to avoid node duplication - create VRFs (or import them via CSV), associate the node with VRF and point duplicated instances to master OSPF RID.

ro_res0: OSPF Watcher - repository and deploy guide
ro1_p0: For each exercise: make one change, predict the OSPF result, observe the Watcher event, then find the same fact in Topolograph Monitoring, in the SDK, and - for the correlation exercises - in the agent's answer. Restore the lab before the next independent exercise.

ro2_p0: Run the public GRE-based ospf01 topology from the OSPF Watcher repository.
ro2_cmd:
cd containerlab/ospf01
sudo clab inspect --all
sudo clab destroy --topo ospf01.clab.yml --cleanup   # only if a stale ospf01 is listed
sudo ./prepare.sh
sudo clab deploy --topo ospf01.clab.yml
sudo docker logs clab-ospf01-ospf-watcher
sudo tail -f watcher/logs/watcher1.ospf.log
ro2_o0: Six router containers plus the watcher are up: `docker ps --filter name=clab-ospf01` lists clab-ospf01-router1..6 and clab-ospf01-ospf-watcher, all State=Up.
ro2_o1: The watcher has the LSDB and is sniffing: `docker logs clab-ospf01-ospf-watcher` shows an "OSPF LSDB received" line and "Start sniffing on interface: eth1".
ro2_o2: Adjacencies are Full: `docker exec clab-ospf01-router1 vtysh -c 'show ip ospf neighbor'` lists each neighbour in Full state; the first Topolograph graph then contains six routers.
ro2_rollback: **Rollback:** When you finish the runbook, remove the lab with `sudo clab destroy --topo ospf01.clab.yml --cleanup` from `containerlab/ospf01/`.
ro3_p0: The runbook uses three event families: host, metric, and network. Read `event_object` as the changed object, `event_status` as the transition, and `event_detected_by` as the advertising or detecting router. `graph_time` is the watcher's own label for the run and selects the Topolograph graph.
ro3_p1: Read the metric line above as one sentence: at `2026-09-06T13:11:04Z` the watcher `ospfwatcher-demo` saw router `10.10.10.2` re-advertise its link toward `10.10.10.3` with the cost changed from 10 to 222, on local interface `192.168.23.1`, in area `0.0.0.0` / AS 12345. The network line right after it carries the same 10 -> 222 move for the subnet `192.168.23.0/24` on that link.
ro3_s1: `area_num` `0.0.0.0` and `asn` 12345 identify the routing domain; `sesid` is the watcher session, `srcid` the source router id.
ro4_p0: One OSPF change produces one Watcher CSV line. Fluent Bit forwards it to Topolograph, which stores it and exposes it through the Monitoring page, the event API, and the SDK. Each exercise below checks the same fact at every level available to you.
ro4_s0: ospf01 Watcher log  ->  Fluent Bit CSV parser  ->  Topolograph ingestion  ->  Monitoring page + event API  ->  Topolograph SDK
ro4_s1: Monitoring page: OSPF/IS-IS Real-Time Monitoring. Choose the graph by its timestamp, set a time window, click Find logs; toggles filter subnet / link / metric events.
ro4_s2: The graph selector on that page lists every topology snapshot the watcher reported, newest first - that is the topology the watcher sent.

ro5_t: 5. Cost change on a point-to-point link
ro5_p0: Change `router2` eth1 toward `router3`. OSPF costs are directed, so the reverse `router3`-to-`router2` cost must not be described as the same scalar.
ro5_cmd:
sudo docker exec clab-ospf01-router2 vtysh \
  -c 'conf t' -c 'interface eth1' -c 'ip ospf cost 222'
ro5_v0_sum: The metric and network lines for the change and its rollback
ro5_v1_path: On OSPF/IS-IS Real-Time Monitoring, pick this graph in Choose the graph, set the From/To window around 13:11 UTC and click Find logs. With Changed metric on, the feed shows one row: object `10.10.10.3`, detected by `10.10.10.2`, 10 -> 222 - the `router2` -> `router3` direction only. The reverse direction is not listed. The topology graph below the feed redraws the `router2`-`router3` link with the new weight.
ro5_v1_sum: The 10 -> 222 metric change on the event feed
ro5_v2_req:
adj = graph.events.get_adjacency_events(
    start_time="2026-09-06T13:11:00Z", end_time="2026-09-06T13:11:10Z")
net = graph.events.get_network_events(
    start_time="2026-09-06T13:11:00Z", end_time="2026-09-06T13:11:10Z")
print(adj["adjacency_cost_change_events"])
print(net["network_cost_change_events"])
e = adj["adjacency_cost_change_events"][0]
print(e.event_object, e.event_detected_by, e.old_cost, e.new_cost, e.local_ip_address)
ro5_v2_note: The metric event names the `router2` -> `router3` direction (`event_object` `10.10.10.3`, `event_detected_by` `10.10.10.2`), cost 10 -> 222; `192.168.23.0/24` carries the same move. The reverse direction is absent from both lists.
ro5_v2_sum: get_adjacency_events and get_network_events return the same object and costs
ro5_v3_prompt: **Prompt:** What happened with router2 in the last 10 minutes?
ro5_v3_a0: In the 06Sep2026_12h31m41s snapshot, router2 (10.10.10.2) had one change in this window - an OSPF metric change on its link to 10.10.10.3, detected by router2 itself. No prefix, link, or node went down.
ro5_v3_a1: 13:11:04 - router2 raised the cost of its link to 10.10.10.3 from 10 to 222 (192.168.23.0/24, area 0).
ro5_v3_a2: 13:11:19 - router2 restored that cost from 222 back to 10.
ro5_v3_a3: Only the router2 -> 10.10.10.3 direction produced an event; the reverse 10.10.10.3 -> router2 direction did not change.
ro5_v3_note: Observed on this run: `router2` re-advertised its link to `router3` at cost 222 (was 10); the reverse `router3` -> `router2` direction did not change.
ro5_v3_sum: A generic incident question about router2

ri_intro: Make one controlled change at a time, predict its effect, then verify the same fact from the Watcher event through Topolograph.
ri_evidence: **Evidence captured 2026-09-07.** Every command below was run by hand against a freshly deployed isis01 lab. The Watcher CSV lines and SDK output are literal captures from that run (graph 07Sep2026_06h49m43s_6_hosts); the agent answer is one real Qwen response.
ri_res0: IS-IS Watcher - repository and deploy guide
ri1_p0: For each exercise: make one change, predict the IS-IS result, observe the Watcher event, then find the same fact in Topolograph Monitoring, in the SDK, and - for the correlation exercise - in the agent's answer. Restore the lab before the next independent exercise.
ri1_p1: isis01 is a six-router FRR domain in one area (`49.0001`, AS `65100`). `router2`-`router3` runs Level-1-2; `router3` to `router6` and `router3`'s leg to the `router4`/`router5` LAN are Level-2-only. The Watcher rides a Level-2 adjacency on `router1` and resolves each System ID to its hostname through the IS-IS dynamic-hostname TLV, so events name `router2`, `router3`, `router6` rather than `0100.1001.000x`.
ri1_s0: The Watcher CSV line is the deterministic source event.
ri1_s1: Monitoring and the SDK prove the event was ingested and is queryable.
ri1_s2: The agent is used only to correlate several events into one incident, never as a replacement for the source line.
ri2_p0: Run the public GRE-based isis01 topology from the IS-IS Watcher repository. `prepare.sh` also creates the `isis-br-dr` bridge and loads the MPLS kernel modules that IS-IS TE needs.
ri2_p1: First check whether a lab is already running with `sudo clab inspect --all`. If a stale isis01 is listed, tear it down with `sudo clab destroy --topo isis01.clab.yml --cleanup` from `containerlab/isis01/` before deploying again - name the topology file so no other lab is touched.
ri2_cmd:
cd containerlab/isis01
sudo clab inspect --all
sudo clab destroy --topo isis01.clab.yml --cleanup   # only if a stale isis01 is listed
sudo ./prepare.sh
sudo clab deploy --topo isis01.clab.yml
sudo docker logs clab-isis01-isis-watcher
sudo tail -f watcher/logs/watcher1.isis.log
ri2_o0: Six router containers plus the watcher are up: `docker ps --filter name=clab-isis01` lists `clab-isis01-router1..6` and `clab-isis01-isis-watcher`, all `State=Up`.
ri2_o1: The watcher has the LSDB and is sniffing: `docker logs clab-isis01-isis-watcher` shows `ISIS LSDB has been received` and `Sniffing packets on interface: eth1`.
ri2_o2: Adjacencies are Up: `docker exec clab-isis01-router1 vtysh -c 'show isis neighbor'` lists `router3` in the `Up` state; the first Topolograph graph then contains six routers.

ri3_p0: The runbook uses three event families: `host`, `metric`, and `network`. Read `event_object` as the changed object, `event_status` as the transition, and `event_detected_by` as the advertising or detecting router. `graph_time` is the watcher's own label for the run and selects the Topolograph graph.
ri3_p1: IS-IS lines carry a `level` field (`1` or `2`) that OSPF lines do not - it is the third field, right after `watcher_name`. Read the `metric` line above as one sentence: at `2026-09-07T06:55:14Z` the watcher `lab-isis01` saw `router3` re-advertise its Level-1 link toward `router2` with the metric changed from `10` to `-1` (adjacency lost), on the interface addressed `192.168.23.2` in area `49.0001` / AS `65100`. The identity behind `router2` is its NET / System ID `49.0001.0100.1001.0002.00`; the watcher prints the hostname because every router advertises the dynamic-hostname TLV.
ri3_p2: A plain `host` or `network` up/down line carries no cost fields, so Fluent Bit forwards only the paired `changed` line. Topolograph reads an adjacency going down from the `metric` line whose `new_cost` is `-1`, and coming back from the one whose `old_cost` is `-1`.
ri3_s1: `area_num` `49.0001` and `asn` `65100` identify the routing domain; `sesid` is the watcher session, `srcid` the source router System ID (`router1`, `0100.1001.0001`).

ri10_t: 10. Reading TE attributes and filtering edges by IS-IS level
ri10_p0: Every parsed link carries its metric and RFC 5305 TE sub-TLVs (admin group, bandwidth pools, TE metric) alongside `isis_level` -- `1` or `2` for a link advertised at one level only, `3` (L1L2) for one advertised at both. `router3`-`router6` is Level-2-only, so it is the one edge on this graph tagged `isis_level: 2`; every other link here is `3`.
ri10_p1: This graph (`18Sep2026_08h50m15s_6_hosts`) came from a full LSDB parse (`POST /graphs` with `router1`'s `show isis database detail`). A Watcher-sourced graph stores per-level TE snapshots the same way, so it answers a level-aware request with real data too.
ri10_alt: The Web edge tooltip for router2-router3, now split into two side-by-side panels -- 0100.1001.0003 to 0100.1001.0002 (Metric 10) on the left and 0100.1001.0002 to 0100.1001.0003 (Metric 50) on the right -- each with its own Local/Remote IP, TE Metric, Bandwidth and Unreserved BW badges, plus the L1/L2 breakdown further down. Before the router2 mpls-te router-address fix (Point-to-point link section rollback note), router2's directed edges landed on two different vertices and this same link showed a single column with one direction missing.
ri10_o0: `isis_level=2` lists exactly one edge per direction on the Level-2-only circuit: `10.10.10.3 -> 10.10.10.6` and `10.10.10.6 -> 10.10.10.3`, both `isis_level: 2` -- no other link in this six-router graph matches.
ri10_o1: `admin_group=0x647a0001` lists 2 edges: `10.10.10.1 -> 10.10.10.3` (cost 10) and `10.10.10.2 -> 10.10.10.3` (cost 50) -- the two directions `router1`/`router2` advertise toward `router3` with that group, each carrying its own `admin_group`, `temetric` and `unreserved_bw_0`..`unreserved_bw_7` fields.
ri10_o2: `temetric__gt=25` lists 2 edges: `10.10.10.1 -> 10.10.10.3` (`temetric: 111111`) and `10.10.10.3 -> 10.10.10.2` (`temetric: 32`) -- the range operator reads the same TE-metric field the Web tooltip's `TE Metric` badge shows.
ri11_t: 11. Computing CSPF for one IS-IS level
ri11_p0: `GET /graph/{graph_time}/cspf-path/{node_a}/{node_b}?level=1|2` answers a question the combined/default calculation cannot: which path, if any, exists using strictly that level's own advertised metrics and TE data. `router3`-`router6` is Level-2-only, so `router6` is not even a member of the Level-1 topology -- a Level-1 request between `router1` and `router6` is not a strict-constraint failure, it is `src/dst not found`.
ri11_p1: Requesting an explicit `level` against a graph that predates per-level storage -- such as one uploaded before per-level snapshots were introduced -- fails closed with `422` and `code: isis_level_calculation_unavailable` rather than silently answering from the merged view.
ri11_o1: `level=1`: `"path": []`, `"reason": "src/dst not found"` -- `router6` has no Level-1 membership at all, on this or any graph, since its only circuit is Level-2-only.
ri11_o2: `level=2`: identical to the combined view here (`"cost": 20`) -- this graph's one Level-1-2 hop, `router1`-`router3`, also advertises at L2, so the L2-only path matches the default one.
ri11_o3: The same request against the pre-per-level graph `12Sep2026_19h04m47s_6_hosts` (`?level=1`) returns `422` with `"code": "isis_level_calculation_unavailable"`, `"action": "reupload_graph"` -- re-run the LSDB upload under the current Topolograph version to get a real per-level answer instead.
ri12_p0: The six-router lab is useful for inspecting Watcher events and TE fields, but it does not provide enough alternative routes for meaningful CSPF exercises. Use the [`13-hosts-demo-isis` lab](https://github.com/Vadims06/topolograph/tree/master/containerlab/13-hosts-demo-isis): deploy it yourself, or skip the deployment and download the ready LSDB [`demo_isis_LSDB.txt`](https://github.com/Vadims06/topolograph/blob/master/demo_isis_LSDB.txt).

ri13_t: 13. Read TE values before computing a path
ri13_p0: Inspect the graph's TE attributes before applying a constraint. Identify the gold and red admin groups, high TE metrics, the small priority-7 bandwidth pool, SRLG-bearing links, and links that are not TE-enabled; a plain shortest-path calculation does not show whether a link is suitable for a tunnel.
ri13_p1: On this graph, gold (`0x00000002`) matches 10 directed edges, red (`0x00000004`) matches 2, `temetric__gt=30` matches 4, `unreserved_bw_7__lt=1000000` matches 2, and `is_te_link=False` returns the two directions of `r110-r111`.
ri13_cmd: # Run from the SDK against the graph uploaded in step 1
ri13_req:
for query in (
    {'admin_group': '0x00000002'},
    {'admin_group': '0x00000004'},
    {'temetric__gt': 30},
    {'unreserved_bw_7__lt': 1_000_000},
    {'is_te_link': False},
):
    result = graph.edges_list(per_page=200, **query)
    print(query, result['pagination']['total'])
ri13_o0: The 8 edges on `r10-r100` and `r100-r110`/`r100-r111` carry SRLG data; the two parallel `r10-r100` links keep their separate groups.
ri13_o1: Passing `is_te_link='yes'` is rejected with HTTP 400: `Wrong type, expected 'boolean'`.
ri14_p0: Calculate the unconstrained path from `r10` to `r14` and keep it as the baseline for the remaining exercises. Each following constraint can then be compared with a known route.
ri14_p1: The reference path is `r10 r100 r110 r14`, with cost 30. It uses the `eth2` parallel link between `r10` and `r100`.
ri14_cmd: # No router change: calculate the reference CSPF path
ri14_o0: The baseline uses IGP metrics. The next four steps deliberately move it with one constraint at a time.
ri15_p0: Use `srlg_exclude` to route around a link or shared duct under maintenance. The reference path `r10 r100 r110 r14` costs 30: its first hop belongs to SRLG 300, while both parallel first hops share SRLG 100.
ri15_p1: Excluding 300 keeps the same routers but selects `eth1`, raising the cost to 35. Excluding 100 gives `r10 r11 r100 r110 r14` at cost 40; excluding 200 gives `r10 r100 r101 r111 r14` at cost 45; excluding both 100 and 200 gives `r10 r11 r101 r111 r14` at cost 50.
ri15_cmd: # No router change: change the excluded risk group in each request
ri15_req:
for groups in ([300], [100], [200], [100, 200]):
    print(groups, graph.cspf_path('r10', 'r14', srlg_exclude=groups))
ri15_o0: The route changes because the constraint removes links, not because any IGP metric changed.
ri16_t: 16. Select a route by bandwidth and setup priority
ri16_p0: Request an 8 Mbit tunnel at different setup priorities. The reference route `r10 r100 r110 r14` costs 30, but `r100-r110` advertises only 4 Mbit in its priority-7 pool and 10 Mbit at priorities 0-3.
ri16_p1: At priority 7, CSPF moves the tunnel to `r10 r100 r111 r14`, cost 40. At priority 0, it keeps `r10 r100 r110 r14`, cost 30. A 20 Mbit request fits on no available path and returns a constraint refusal.
ri16_cmd: # No router change: vary bandwidth and setup_priority
ri16_o0: Setup priority selects the advertised unreserved-bandwidth pool used for placement; it does not alter the route's IGP cost.
ri17_p0: Recalculate the path with `metric_type='te'` after checking that every candidate link carries a TE metric. The IGP path `r10 r100 r110 r14` costs 30, but `r100-r110` has TE metric 100 while `r100-r111` has TE metric 10.
ri17_p1: CSPF selects `r10 r100 r111 r14` with TE cost 30. The same path has IGP cost 40, which makes the effect of the selected metric visible.
ri17_cmd: # No router change: select TE cost instead of IGP cost
ri17_o0: If a candidate link has no TE metric, CSPF falls back to IGP for that calculation; inspect the edge attributes first.
ri18_p0: Use admin-group bits to require or avoid link classes. Bit 1 is gold and bit 2 is red. The unconstrained path from `r13` to `r15` is `r13 r100 r110 r15`, cost 30.
ri18_p1: Requiring gold with `admin_include_all=['1']` changes that path to `r13 r101 r111 r15`, cost 45; from `r10` to `r14`, it gives `r10 r101 r111 r14`, cost 55. Avoiding red with `admin_exclude_any=['2']` gives `r13 r100 r111 r15`, cost 40.
ri18_cmd: # No router change: admin groups are bit numbers, not hexadecimal mask values
ri18_req:
print(graph.cspf_path('r13', 'r15', admin_include_all=['1']))
print(graph.cspf_path('r10', 'r14', admin_include_all=['1']))
print(graph.cspf_path('r13', 'r15', admin_exclude_any=['2']))
ri18_o0: Bit 1 means mask `0x00000002`; bit 2 means mask `0x00000004`. Bit 0 is the least significant bit.
ri19_t: 19. Restrict CSPF to one IS-IS level
ri19_p0: Set `level=1` or `level=2` to calculate inside one IS-IS topology and verify that both endpoints belong to it. Between `r30` and `r31`, the direct Level-1 path costs 10, while the Level-2 path `r30 r10 r11 r31` costs 40.
ri19_p1: The `r130`-`r131` path costs 10 at Level 1 but returns `src/dst not found` at Level 2. The combined topology has an `r130`-`r15` path of cost 50, but neither individual level has that path because it crosses the level boundary.
ri19_cmd: # No router change: constrain the request to Level 1 or Level 2
ri19_o0: An explicit level request on a graph stored before per-level data returns HTTP 422 with `code: isis_level_calculation_unavailable`; it must be reuploaded.
ri20_t: 20. Distinguish an unsatisfied constraint from a missing endpoint
ri20_p0: Read `reason` whenever CSPF returns an empty `path`. The 20 Mbit request from step 5 has valid endpoints but no path with enough bandwidth, while a Level-1 request from `r130` to `r15` has no single-level topology containing both endpoints.
ri20_p1: The bandwidth request returns `no path satisfies the requested constraints`; the wrong-level request returns `src/dst not found`. These failures require different corrective actions.
ri20_cmd: # Repeat the failed requests from steps 5 and 8
ri20_out:
{'cost': None, 'path': [], 'reason': 'no path satisfies the requested constraints'}
{'cost': None, 'path': [], 'reason': 'src/dst not found'}
ri20_o0: The first reason calls for relaxing bandwidth, affinity, or SRLG constraints; the second means the requested topology does not contain both endpoints.
ri21_p0: Model maintenance on `r100-r110` without changing the routers. On a disposable graph, use `update_edge` to add SRLG 999 to the Level-2 edge, recalculate while excluding that group, and then clear the SRLG.
ri21_p1: Excluding 999 changes the path from `r10 r100 r110 r14`, cost 30, to `r10 r100 r111 r14`, cost 40; clearing the SRLG restores the reference path. A Level-2-only edge rejects `isis_level=1`. Because `replace_edge` removes per-level data, an explicit-level CSPF request returns HTTP 422 after a full replacement.

# Run this on a disposable graph: the edit is persistent
# Find the edge id first with edges_list(include=['edge_key'])
ri21_req:
edge = next(e for e in graph.edges_list(include=['edge_key'], per_page=200)['items']
             if e['src'] == 'r100' and e['dst'] == 'r110')
print(graph.update_edge(edge['id'], isis_level=2, srlg=[999]))
print(graph.cspf_path('r10', 'r14', srlg_exclude=[999]))
print(graph.update_edge(edge['id'], isis_level=2, srlg=[]))
print(graph.cspf_path('r10', 'r14'))
ri21_o0: `update_edge` is partial; `replace_edge` is a full rewrite. Do not use either on the reference graph you want to keep unchanged.

rg_visibility_intro: A BMP session established with a route reflector does not automatically provide a view of every RR client's table. A BMP session capable of exporting Loc-RIB provides the most accurate view of routing-table state. Topolograph can also work with explicit assumptions when some information is unavailable. For example, a device's RIB state can be inferred from a neighboring BMP speaker's RFC 8671 Adj-RIB-Out post-policy toward that device, even when no BMP session is established with the device itself.

rg_open_card: Open in Topolograph: demo graph, router card
rg_node_card_intro: The route count in the device form shows the RIB view for that router: either its Loc-RIB received through a BMP session with the device, or Adj-RIB-Out post-policy received through a BMP session with a neighboring device.
rg_node_card_steps_0: Click 123.14.14.14 (PE14) on the graph and find the BGP section in the device form.
rg_node_card_steps_1: Confirm Routes is 4 and read the explanation: the routes were advertised by 123.123.101.101 (RR2) to this router through RFC 8671.
rg_node_card_steps_2: Read the RIB breakdown. Adj-RIB-Out post-policy describes 123.123.101.101 (RR2)'s exported RIB; from 123.14.14.14 (PE14)'s perspective these four advertisements are its inferred Adj-RIB-In.
rg_node_card_steps_3: The Adj-RIB-Out (post) 4 row is included in Routes: it is 123.123.101.101 (RR2)'s Adj-RIB-Out toward 123.14.14.14 (PE14), used as 123.14.14.14 (PE14)'s inferred Adj-RIB-In.
rg_node_card_visual: This form shows the RIB view for 123.14.14.14 (PE14): four routes from Adj-RIB-Out post-policy received through BMP from 123.123.101.101 (RR2).
rg_node_card_alt: 123.14.14.14 (PE14) device form showing four routes advertised by 123.123.101.101 (RR2) and Adj-RIB-Out post-policy data

rg_routes_title: 6. Filtering, sorting, and pagination for one node's routes
rg_open_device: Open in Topolograph: demo graph, router card
rg_routes_intro: Open the route table from the device form; the table retains the RIB scope selected for 123.14.14.14 (PE14).
rg_routes_steps_1: Filter prefix by 100.30.0.0/24. Matching rows and the table counter must both fall from 4 to 1.
rg_routes_steps_2: Clear the prefix filter and inspect other attributes independently: local pref = 250 leaves two VPN routes, afi = 2 leaves two IPv6 routes, and med = 20 leaves two routes from 123.123.30.30 (PE30).
rg_routes_steps_3: Clear filters and confirm all four 123.14.14.14 (PE14) routes return. Clearing a table filter must not remove the device scope established by the form.
rg_routes_steps_4: Click a sortable heading such as prefix, nexthop, local pref, or med. Repeated clicks cycle ascending, descending, and unsorted; address columns use address order, not text order.
rg_routes_steps_5: Use Rows per page for large route tables. The demo has only one page in this node-scoped example, so the previous and next controls correctly remain disabled.
rg_routes_visual: The table below retains the 123.14.14.14 (PE14) scope and adds the prefix filter, leaving one matching route.
rg_routes_alt: 123.14.14.14 (PE14) route table filtered from four routes to the prefix 100.30.0.0/24
rg_routes_result: The filtered row shows 123.123.101.101 (RR2) as bmp source and Adj-RIB-Out post-policy as the observed RIB.
rg_open_path: Open in Topolograph: demo graph, BGP routes tab
rg_best_path_intro: For each prefix, the demo demonstrates one best-path selection criterion. Start with AS_PATH: compare the candidate attributes, then build the route from 123.123.101.101 (RR2) and verify the selected BGP next hop.
rg_as_path_steps_1: Compare the two candidates: both have `Local Preference` 100, `Origin` IGP, and `MED` 10. 123.123.30.30 (PE30) advertises `AS_PATH` 65010 65011 65012; 123.14.14.14 (PE14) advertises `AS_PATH` 65010.
rg_as_path_steps_2: Switch to BGP / VPN path mode. Set Router to 123.123.101.101 (RR2), VPN or global table to global, and To to 198.18.2.0/24; then select Build a path.
rg_as_path_steps_3: In Route resolution, confirm the first row is BGP on 123.123.101.101 (RR2) with next hop 123.14.14.14 (PE14). The remaining rows resolve that selected next hop through IGP.
rg_as_path_candidates_alt: BGP route filters and the two AS_PATH candidates for 198.18.2.0/24
rg_as_path_builder_visual: Next, select the BGP / VPN path form and enter 123.123.101.101 (RR2), the global table, and this prefix.
rg_as_path_builder_alt: BGP VPN path form set to 123.123.101.101 (RR2), the global table, and 198.18.2.0/24
rg_as_path_resolution_visual: In Route resolution, the first row shows 123.123.101.101 (RR2) selecting 123.14.14.14 (PE14) as the BGP next hop; the following rows are built from OSPF data.
rg_as_path_result_alt: Route resolution showing 123.123.101.101 (RR2)'s BGP decision with 123.14.14.14 (PE14) as the selected next hop
rg_as_path_result: The post-policy candidates differ in AS_PATH length while Local Preference, Origin, and MED tie. Building the route from 123.123.101.101 (RR2) selects 123.14.14.14 (PE14) as the BGP next hop; the following IGP rows show reachability to that BGP next hop.

rg_dec_r4c3: Different neighboring AS values make MED ineligible

rg_advanced_text: The demo shows the six BGP best-path selection criteria listed in the table above. It does not demonstrate selection of eBGP over iBGP, IGP cost to the next hop, route age, cluster-list length, or BGP neighbor address.
rg_open_compare: Open in Topolograph: demo graph, BGP routes tab, Compare
rg_compare_intro: Live shows the current route-table state. Compare evaluates route state at T0 and T1.
rg_compare_steps_0: Open the graph-wide BGP Routes table and switch from Live to Compare.
rg_compare_steps_1: Keep the default one-hour T0 to T1 window created when the demo loads, then press Run. The window also holds the MAC move from the EVPN section, so set the Prefix filter to Equals 100.14.210.0/24.
rg_compare_steps_2: The table shows one added route, 100.14.210.0/24; changed at contains the time of its last change before T1.
rg_compare_steps_3: added means the route is absent at T0 and present at T1; withdrawn means it is present at T0 and absent at T1; changed means it is present at both instants but its attributes differ. Events after T1 are outside the comparison.
rg_compare_steps_4: Switch back to Live to open the current route-table state.
rg_compare_visual: The comparison below is the endpoint difference for the default demo window, not a chronological event log.
rg_compare_alt: BGP route Compare mode showing 100.14.210.0/24 as added in the default one-hour window
rg_compare_result: For the default demo interval, route 100.14.210.0/24 has status added and MED 80 at T1.
rg_events_intro: Events uses the same BGP Routes drawer and time range, but preserves every route and peer observation instead of reducing them to a T0-to-T1 difference.
rg_events_steps_0: Switch from Compare to Events and keep a time window that covers the demo change burst. Press Clear filters first: the Prefix filter from Compare would hide the MAC move and the peer-down event.
rg_events_steps_1: Press Run. The last three rows are one route add, one peer down event, and one route change for 100.14.210.0/24; the rows above them are the MAC move from the EVPN section.
rg_events_steps_2: Use event, kind, prefix, peer source, peer target, and at to distinguish route changes from BGP-session state changes.
rg_events_visual: The Events view below lists the observations chronologically: the end of the MAC move, then the added route, the peer-down event, and the changed route with MED 80.
rg_events_alt: BGP Routes Events mode showing a route add, a peer down event, and a route change
rg_events_result: Events shows all three observations in order. Unlike Compare, it keeps intermediate events even when the final route state is unchanged.
rg_open_resolution: Open in Topolograph: demo graph, Standard / IGP path mode
rg_resolution_intro: BGP chooses the route; OSPF supplies reachability to the selected BGP next hop. The path view shows that handoff explicitly.
rg_resolution_steps_0: In Standard / IGP path mode, use 123.123.30.30 (PE30) as the source and 100.14.0.0/24 as the destination.
rg_resolution_steps_1: Inspect the selected BGP row and identify 123.14.14.14 (PE14) as the BGP next hop.
rg_resolution_steps_2: Open Route resolution and read the result from left to right: the first row is BGP with administrative distance 200 and next hop 123.14.14.14 (PE14).
rg_resolution_steps_3: Continue through the five IGP rows with administrative distance 110 that physically resolve reachability from 123.123.30.30 (PE30) to 123.14.14.14 (PE14).
rg_resolution_visual: The table below separates the single BGP route choice from the IGP hops that make its next hop reachable.
rg_resolution_alt: Route resolution table with one BGP decision followed by five IGP next-hop-resolution rows
rg_resolution_result: The BGP next hop points to 123.14.14.14 (PE14); the rest of the route is then built from OSPF data.
rg_limits_intro: Filter for 123.123.31.31 (PE31). Topolograph can show the routes that 123.123.100.100 (RR1) received from 123.123.31.31 (PE31), but RFC 7854 alone does not reveal which route 123.123.31.31 (PE31) installed or what 123.123.100.100 (RR1) advertised back to it.
rg_limits_steps_0: Open BGP Routes and filter the peer ip column by 123.123.31.31. Adj-RIB-In (pre) and Adj-RIB-In (post) show routes that 123.123.100.100 (RR1) received from 123.123.31.31 (PE31), not 123.123.31.31 (PE31)'s routing table.
rg_limits_steps_1: Open the BGP / VPN path form and select Router 123.123.31.31. The form warns that this router's table is not observed and does not allow a path to be built from BGP data.
rg_limits_steps_2: Compare 123.123.31.31 (PE31) with 123.15.15.15 (PE15): for 123.15.15.15 (PE15), Topolograph uses 123.123.101.101 (RR2) Loc-RIB and explicitly assumes that 123.123.101.101 (RR2) advertised the route to 123.15.15.15 (PE15) and 123.15.15.15 (PE15) applied its inbound policy.
rg_limits_result: Topolograph does not build a path when the available BMP data does not describe the selected device's routing table. To remove this limit, provide the device's Loc-RIB through RFC 9069 or its per-neighbor Adj-RIB-Out post-policy through RFC 8671.
rg_evpn_title: 11. EVPN: where a host is, which leaves carry a VNI, MAC moves
rg_open_evpn: Open in Topolograph: demo graph, BGP / VPN path mode
rg_evpn_intro: The demo also holds a BGP EVPN/VXLAN fabric captured on the 13-hosts-demo-bgp lab: leaves 123.14.14.14, 123.15.15.15, 123.123.30.30 and 123.123.31.31, each using its router ID as VTEP, L2VNI 1010 on all four and L2VNI 1020 on 123.123.30.30 and 123.123.31.31, and VRF tenant1 with L3VNI 5000. Both route reflectors export it over BMP.
rg_evpn_vni_steps_0: Switch to BGP / VPN path mode and leave Router empty. VPN or global table then lists every VNI and VRF of the fabric.
rg_evpn_vni_steps_1: Choose 65000:1020 · VNI 1020. The graph highlights 123.123.30.30 and 123.123.31.31, and the form reports Leaves with this VPN: 2.
rg_evpn_vni_steps_2: Press Colour underlay to paint the IGP path between these leaves: the links that carry VNI 1020 between its VTEPs.
rg_evpn_vni_alt: BGP / VPN form with no router and VNI 1020 chosen, reporting two leaves
rg_evpn_underlay_alt: Graph with the IGP path between the two VNI 1020 leaves painted
rg_evpn_leaf_steps_0: Click 123.123.30.30 on the graph. The EVPN section of the device form shows its VTEP and three counts: L2VNI 2, ESI 1 and MAC/IP 2.
rg_evpn_leaf_steps_1: The counts cover only what this VTEP originates, so the form stays short on a leaf with thousands of VNIs. ESI is hidden on a leaf without multihoming, as on 123.14.14.14.
rg_evpn_leaf_steps_2: Click L2VNI. Graph table opens BGP Routes with one row per VNI, 1010 and 1020, filtered by the leaf's VTEP. ESI and MAC/IP open its Ethernet Segments and hosts the same way.
rg_evpn_leaf_alt: Device form of 123.123.30.30 with the EVPN section: VTEP 123.123.30.30, L2VNI 2, ESI 1, MAC/IP 2
rg_evpn_leaf_vni_alt: Graph table with the two L2VNIs of VTEP 123.123.30.30
rg_evpn_host_steps_0: Set Router to 123.15.15.15 and VPN or global table to tenant1.
rg_evpn_host_steps_1: Type 10.10.20.13 into To. Graph table opens BGP Routes with the host's row: VTEP 123.123.31.31, VNI 1020, L3VNI 5000 and MAC 00:c1:ab:00:00:03.
rg_evpn_host_steps_2: Press Build a path. The IGP path from 123.15.15.15 to VTEP 123.123.31.31 is painted: the host exists only in the overlay, so the path ends at its VTEP.
rg_evpn_host_alt: BGP / VPN form and Graph table with host 10.10.20.13 behind VTEP 123.123.31.31
rg_evpn_host_note: 123.15.15.15 carries VNI 1010 but not VNI 1020, so it reaches this host through VRF tenant1 (symmetric IRB, L3VNI 5000), not through the VNI.
rg_evpn_move_steps_0: Set Router to 123.123.101.101 and VPN or global table to 65000:1010 · VNI 1010.
rg_evpn_move_steps_1: Type the MAC 00:c1:ab:00:00:01 into To. Graph table shows its current VTEP 123.15.15.15. Switch the table to Events and press Run, then type 123.14.14.14 into the Moved from VTEP filter: the remaining row is the move itself, the add on 123.15.15.15 with its time.
rg_evpn_move_steps_2: A move is the MAC leaving one VTEP and appearing on another. The same MAC advertised by several VTEPs under one ESI is multihoming, not a move.
rg_evpn_move_alt: Events of MAC 00:c1:ab:00:00:01: the add on VTEP 123.15.15.15, moved from 123.14.14.14
rg_evpn_mh_steps_0: Keep Router 123.123.101.101 and VNI 1010, and type 00:c1:ab:00:00:02 into To.
rg_evpn_mh_steps_1: Graph table lists the MAC on two VTEPs, 123.123.30.30 and 123.123.31.31, with one ESI 03:44:38:39:ff:00:01:00:00:01: the host is attached to both leaves through one Ethernet Segment.
rg_evpn_mh_steps_2: Press Build a path. The paths to both VTEPs are painted at once. If one leaf fails, the other still serves the segment; which leaf forwards broadcast traffic (the designated forwarder) is decided on the leaves and is not visible over BMP.
rg_evpn_mh_alt: Graph table with MAC 00:c1:ab:00:00:02 on two VTEPs and one ESI
rg_evpn_mh_path_alt: Graph with the paths from 123.123.101.101 to both VTEPs of the Ethernet Segment
rg_evpn_l3_steps_0: Open Graph table, select BGP Routes and filter evpn route type by 5.
rg_evpn_l3_steps_1: The table lists the IP Prefix routes of VRF tenant1: 10.10.10.0/24 from all four leaves and 10.10.20.0/24 from 123.123.30.30 and 123.123.31.31, each with L3VNI 5000 and its leaf as the VTEP.
rg_evpn_result: Every answer comes from the BMP feed of the route reflectors, resolved onto the OSPF graph: a VTEP is the leaf with that router ID, and a path to a host ends at its VTEP.
